statement: Let $f^*\colon\mathcal D\to\mathcal C$ be a strong monoidal functor between [closed monoidal categories](c:closed-monoidal-category), with a left [adjoint](c:adjoint-functor) $f_!$. For $B\in\mathcal D$, the projection morphism $\pi_{A,B}\colon f_!(A\otimes f^*B)\to f_!A\otimes B$ is invertible for every $A$ if and only if $\kappa_{B,E}\colon f^*[B,E]\to[f^*B,f^*E]$ is invertible for every $E$.

hypotheses.text: The categories $\mathcal C$ and $\mathcal D$ are [closed monoidal](c:closed-monoidal-category): each functor $-\otimes B$ has a right adjoint $[B,-]$.
The functor $f^*$ is strong monoidal, with isomorphisms $\varphi\colon f^*X\otimes f^*Y\cong f^*(X\otimes Y)$.
The functor $f^*$ has a left [adjoint](c:adjoint-functor) $f_!$ with unit $\eta$.

conclusion: For fixed $B$, the morphism $\pi_{A,B}$ is invertible for every $A\in\mathcal C$ exactly when $\kappa_{B,E}$ is invertible for every $E\in\mathcal D$.

proofs.name: Mate and Yoneda
proofs.slogan: Turn maps out of both sides into maps into $[f^*B,f^*E]$ and $f^*[B,E]$, show that $\pi$ becomes $\kappa$, then compare by the Yoneda lemma.
proofs.scope: The criterion for a fixed $B$, with $A$ over $\mathcal C$ and $E$ over $\mathcal D$. The projection morphism need not be invertible for a general $f^*$; the proof shows exactly when it is.

roles.why: Internal homs turn maps out of tensor products into maps into hom objects.
The isomorphisms $\varphi$ define $\pi$ and $\kappa$ and make the two translations agree.
The adjunction $f_!\dashv f^*$ moves maps out of $f_!$ to maps into $f^*$.

steps.slogan: Define the projection morphism $\pi$ and the comparison map $\kappa$.
steps.detail: The map $\pi_{A,B}$ is the adjunct of $A\otimes f^*B\xrightarrow{\eta_A\otimes1}f^*f_!A\otimes f^*B\xrightarrow{\varphi}f^*(f_!A\otimes B)$. The map $\kappa_{B,E}$ is the adjunct of $f^*[B,E]\otimes f^*B\xrightarrow{\varphi}f^*([B,E]\otimes B)\xrightarrow{f^*\mathrm{ev}}f^*E$.

steps.slogan: Rewrite maps out of $f_!(A\otimes f^*B)$ as maps from $A$ into $[f^*B,f^*E]$.
steps.detail: The adjunction gives $\mathrm{Hom}(f_!(A\otimes f^*B),E)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(A\otimes f^*B,f^*E)$. Closedness of $\mathcal C$ turns this into $\mathrm{Hom}(A,[f^*B,f^*E])$. Both bijections are natural in $E$.

steps.slogan: Rewrite maps out of $f_!A\otimes B$ as maps from $A$ into $f^*[B,E]$.
steps.detail: Closedness of $\mathcal D$ gives $\mathrm{Hom}(f_!A\otimes B,E)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(f_!A,[B,E])$. The adjunction gives $\mathrm{Hom}(A,f^*[B,E])$. Both bijections are natural in $E$.

steps.slogan: Check that precomposition with $\pi$ becomes postcomposition with $\kappa$.
steps.detail: Take $u\colon f_!A\otimes B\to E$ with adjunct $\hat u\colon A\to f^*[B,E]$. Both $u\circ\pi$ and $\kappa\circ\hat u$ correspond to $f^*(u)\circ\varphi\circ(\eta_A\otimes1)\colon A\otimes f^*B\to f^*E$, by naturality of $\varphi$ and the definition of $\kappa$.

steps.slogan: Compare the two representable functors in $E$ and in $A$ by the Yoneda lemma.
steps.detail: If every $\kappa_{B,E}$ is invertible, then precomposition with $\pi_{A,B}$ is bijective for every $E$, so $\pi_{A,B}$ is invertible by Yoneda in $\mathcal D$. Conversely, if every $\pi_{A,B}$ is invertible, then $\kappa_{B,E}$ induces a bijection on $\mathrm{Hom}(A,-)$ for every $A$, so $\kappa_{B,E}$ is invertible by Yoneda in $\mathcal C$.

concepts.c:closed-monoidal-category: Internal homs turn maps out of tensor products into maps into hom objects.
concepts.c:adjoint-functor: The adjunction moves maps out of $f_!$ to maps into $f^*$.

source.note: The mate correspondence and the Yoneda lemma; the criterion says that the projection morphism is invertible exactly when $f^*$ preserves internal homs out of $B$.

statement: Let $K$ be an [algebraically closed field](c:algebraically-closed-field) of characteristic $0$. The union $\bigcup_{N\ge1}K((x^{1/N}))$ of the fields of Laurent [formal power series](c:formal-power-series) in $x^{1/N}$ (the Puiseux series) is algebraically closed.

hypotheses.text: The field $K$ is [algebraically closed](c:algebraically-closed-field).
The field $K$ has characteristic $0$.

conclusion: Every nonconstant polynomial over the Puiseux field has a root in the Puiseux field.

proofs.name: Shift, rescale and Hensel
proofs.slogan: Induct on the degree, shift and rescale a monic polynomial until its reduction has two coprime factors, then lift them by Hensel's lemma.
proofs.scope: Monic polynomials of degree $n\ge2$ over the Puiseux field $P$; degree 1 is trivial. The valuation $v$ of a series is the exponent of its lowest term.

roles.why: It splits the reduced polynomial over $K$ into linear factors.
It makes $n$ invertible, which allows the shift and forces a repeated root to be $0$.

steps.slogan: Put the coefficients in one field $K((t))$ and induct on the degree.
steps.detail: A monic $P(y)$ of degree $n$ has finitely many coefficients, so all lie in $K((t))$ with $t=x^{1/N}$ for some $N$. Assume that every polynomial of degree below $n$ over the Puiseux field has a root.

steps.slogan: Remove the $y^{n-1}$ term by the substitution $y\mapsto y-a_{n-1}/n$.
steps.detail: The integer $n$ is invertible in characteristic $0$, so the shift keeps the coefficients in $K((t))$. If all remaining coefficients vanish, the polynomial is $y^n$ with the root $0$. Otherwise continue.

steps.slogan: Rescale $y$ by the slope of the [Newton polygon](c:newton-polygon) edge that ends at $(n,0)$.
steps.detail: Let $\mu=\min v(a_i)/(n-i)$ over $i<n$ with $a_i\ne0$. Put $y=x^{\mu}z$ and divide by $x^{n\mu}$. The result $Q$ is monic with coefficients in $\mathcal O=K[[x^{1/N'}]]$ for a suitable $N'$, has no $z^{n-1}$ term, and has a coefficient of valuation $0$.

steps.slogan: Reduce $Q$ modulo the maximal ideal and find two coprime monic factors.
steps.detail: The reduction $\bar Q\in K[z]$ is monic of degree $n$, has no $z^{n-1}$ term and differs from $z^n$. Over $K$ it splits as $\prod(z-r_i)$. If all $r_i$ equal $r$, then $-nr=0$ gives $r=0$ and $\bar Q=z^n$, which is false. So $\bar Q=g_0h_0$ with coprime monic factors of positive degree.

steps.slogan: Lift the factorization to $\mathcal O$ and use the induction hypothesis.
steps.detail: The ring $\mathcal O=K[[t]]$ is complete, so Hensel's lemma lifts $\bar Q=g_0h_0$ to $Q=gh$ with monic $g,h$ of positive degree. Undoing the rescaling and the shift factors $P$ into two monic polynomials of smaller degree. By induction $g$ has a root, which is a root of $P$.

concepts.c:algebraically-closed-field: It gives the roots of the reduced polynomial over $K$.
concepts.c:formal-power-series: The coefficients are Laurent series, where valuations and Hensel's lemma apply.
concepts.c:newton-polygon: Its edge slope gives the scaling that makes the polynomial integral.

source.note: The classical Newton-Puiseux argument by a Tschirnhaus shift, a rescaling by the Newton polygon slope and Hensel's lemma.

statement: Let $R$ be an [integral domain](c:integral-domain) and $p=a_nX^n+\dots+a_0\in R[X]$ with $a_n\ne0$. Suppose $p$ has $n$ [roots](c:root-of-a-polynomial) $r_1,\dots,r_n$ in $R$, counted with multiplicity. Then $a_k=a_n(-1)^{n-k}e_{n-k}(r_1,\dots,r_n)$ for $0\le k\le n$, where $e_j$ is the $j$-th [elementary symmetric polynomial](c:elementary-symmetric-polynomial).

hypotheses.text: The ring $R$ is an [integral domain](c:integral-domain).
The polynomial $p$ has $n=\deg p$ [roots](c:root-of-a-polynomial) in $R$, counted with multiplicity.
The index $k$ satisfies $0\le k\le n$.

formal.difference: The declaration also covers $p=0$ (natural degree $0$), and it writes the roots as the multiset p.roots and the sum of products as esymm.

proofs.name: Factor and expand
proofs.slogan: Factor $p$ over its roots, expand the product, and read off the coefficient of $X^k$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. For $n=0$ the product is empty and the formula reads $a_0=a_0$.

roles.why: Roots of a product add up only in a domain, which makes the factorization over the roots valid.
Having $n$ roots gives a full factorization into $n$ linear factors.
The inequality $k\le n$ makes $n-k$ a valid size of a subset of the roots.

steps.slogan: Factor $p$ as $a_n\prod_{i}(X-r_i)$.
steps.detail: By the factor theorem, $p=(X-r_1)q$. In an integral domain the roots of $p$ are $r_1$ together with the roots of $q$, so $q$ has the other $n-1$ roots and degree $n-1$. Induction on $n$ gives $p=c\prod(X-r_i)$, and comparing leading coefficients gives $c=a_n$.

steps.slogan: Expand the product by choosing $X$ or $-r_i$ in each factor.
steps.detail: A term of $\prod(X-r_i)$ takes $X$ or $-r_i$ from each factor. It has degree $k$ when it takes $-r_i$ from exactly $n-k$ factors. So the coefficient of $X^k$ is the sum of $\prod_{i\in S}(-r_i)$ over the subsets $S$ with $|S|=n-k$.

steps.slogan: Pull the sign out of each product of $n-k$ roots.
steps.detail: Each product $\prod_{i\in S}(-r_i)$ equals $(-1)^{n-k}\prod_{i\in S}r_i$ because $|S|=n-k$. Summing over $S$ gives $(-1)^{n-k}e_{n-k}(r_1,\dots,r_n)$.

steps.slogan: Multiply by the leading coefficient $a_n$ to get $a_k$.
steps.detail: By the factorization, $a_k$ is $a_n$ times the coefficient of $X^k$ in $\prod(X-r_i)$. That coefficient is $(-1)^{n-k}e_{n-k}(r_1,\dots,r_n)$, so $a_k=a_n(-1)^{n-k}e_{n-k}(r_1,\dots,r_n)$.

concepts.c:integral-domain: Roots of a product are the union of the roots of the factors only in a domain.
concepts.c:root-of-a-polynomial: The $n$ roots give the linear factors $X-r_i$.
concepts.c:elementary-symmetric-polynomial: The coefficients of the expanded product are these polynomials in the roots.

source.note: mathlib rewrites p as C p.leadingCoeff * prod (X - C r) over p.roots (C_leadingCoeff_mul_prod_multiset_X_sub_C), then reads off the coefficient with Multiset.prod_X_sub_C_coeff.

statement: Finite graphs are well-quasi-ordered by the [graph minor](c:graph-minor) relation: every infinite sequence $G_1,G_2,\dots$ of finite graphs has indices $i<j$ such that $G_i$ is a minor of $G_j$.

hypotheses.text: The graphs $G_1,G_2,\dots$ are finite and undirected.

conclusion: Some $G_i$ is a minor of a later graph $G_j$, with $i<j$.

proofs.name: Minimal bad sequence and tree structure
proofs.slogan: Choose a minimal bad sequence, use the structure of graphs without a fixed minor, and finish with Kruskal's tree theorem for labelled trees.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof, Graph Minors XX and the papers it builds on. The steps that rest on those papers say so.

roles.why: Finite graphs have sizes, so a minimal bad sequence exists, and they have tree decompositions.

steps.slogan: Assume a bad sequence exists and choose a minimal one.
steps.detail: A sequence is bad when no $G_i$ is a minor of a later $G_j$. Choose a bad sequence with $G_1$ of least size, then $G_2$ of least size among bad sequences that start with $G_1$, and so on. Then no $G_j$ with $j\ge2$ has $G_1$ as a minor. Minimality also makes the proper minors of all $G_j$ well-quasi-ordered.

steps.slogan: Bound the tree-width if $G_1$ is [planar](c:planar-graph) and use Graph Minors IV.
steps.detail: If $G_1$ is planar, the grid theorem (Graph Minors V) bounds the tree-width of every graph without a $G_1$ minor. Graphs of bounded tree-width are well-quasi-ordered by minors (Graph Minors IV, built on Kruskal's tree theorem), which contradicts badness.

steps.slogan: Decompose each graph without a $G_1$ minor into nearly embeddable pieces.
steps.detail: If $G_1$ is not planar, the structure theorem of Graph Minors XVI, with the vortex theory of Graph Minors XVII, gives each such graph a [tree](c:tree) decomposition of bounded adhesion. Each torso is embedded in a surface of bounded genus after removing a bounded number of vertices and adding vortices of bounded width.

steps.slogan: Show that the nearly embedded pieces are well-quasi-ordered with their attachment vertices as roots.
steps.detail: Graph Minors XIX proves well-quasi-ordering for graphs on a fixed surface with rooted vertices. Graph Minors XX extends the argument to the pieces of the structure theorem, and uses the minimality of the sequence.

steps.slogan: Encode each graph as a labelled tree of pieces and order the trees by Kruskal's theorem.
steps.detail: Label each node of the decomposition tree by its piece and its attachment data, labels that form a well-quasi-order by the previous step. Kruskal's tree theorem for labelled trees gives $i<j$ and a label-respecting embedding of the tree of $G_i$ into the tree of $G_j$. The embedding assembles a minor model of $G_i$ in $G_j$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two cases to contradict the bad sequence.
steps.detail: In both cases some $G_i$ is a minor of a later $G_j$, which contradicts badness. So no bad sequence exists, and every infinite sequence of finite graphs has such a pair.

concepts.c:graph-minor: The sequence is bad exactly when no graph is a minor of a later one.
concepts.c:planar-graph: A planar excluded minor forces bounded tree-width.
concepts.c:tree: The tree decomposition turns the graph into a labelled tree.

source.ref: N. Robertson and P. D. Seymour, Graph Minors. XX. Wagner's conjecture, Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B 92 (2004), 325-357
source.note: The outline follows the published proof; steps 2 to 4 rest on Graph Minors IV, V, XVI, XVII and XIX.

statement: Let $A$ be a square matrix with all entries positive. Then there are [diagonal matrices](c:diagonal-matrix) $D_1,D_2$ with positive diagonal such that $D_1AD_2$ is [doubly stochastic](c:doubly-stochastic-matrix). The pair is unique up to $(D_1,D_2)\mapsto(cD_1,c^{-1}D_2)$ with $c>0$.

hypotheses.text: The matrix $A$ is $n\times n$ with $n\ge1$.
Every entry $a_{ij}$ of $A$ is positive.

conclusion: Positive diagonal matrices $D_1,D_2$ make $D_1AD_2$ doubly stochastic, and any two such pairs differ by $(cD_1,c^{-1}D_2)$ with $c>0$.

proofs.name: Relative entropy minimization
proofs.slogan: Minimize the relative entropy over doubly stochastic matrices, show that the minimizer has the form $D_1AD_2$, and use strict convexity for uniqueness.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Doubly stochastic means nonnegative entries with every row sum and column sum equal to $1$.

roles.why: The set of $n\times n$ doubly stochastic matrices is the compact set where the minimum is taken.
Positive entries make $\log(b_{ij}/a_{ij})$ finite and give the diagonal scaling its positive factors.

steps.slogan: Set up the compact convex set of doubly stochastic matrices and the entropy functional.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal D$ be the set of doubly stochastic $n\times n$ matrices. It is a nonempty [compact convex set](c:compact-convex-set) that contains $J/n$, where $J$ is the all-ones matrix. Define $\Phi(B)=\sum_{ij}b_{ij}\log(b_{ij}/a_{ij})$ with $0\log0=0$. Since $t\mapsto t\log t$ is strictly convex, $\Phi$ is continuous and [strictly convex](c:strictly-convex-function) on $\mathcal D$.

steps.slogan: Take a minimizer $B$ of $\Phi$ on $\mathcal D$.
steps.detail: The function $\Phi$ is continuous on the nonempty compact set $\mathcal D$, so it attains its minimum at some $B\in\mathcal D$.

steps.slogan: Show that the minimizer has no zero entry.
steps.detail: Suppose some $b_{ij}=0$. Put $B_t=(1-t)B+tJ/n\in\mathcal D$. Each entry with $b_{kl}=0$ contributes $\frac tn\log\frac t{na_{kl}}$, whose slope tends to $-\infty$ as $t\to0^+$, and the other entries have finite slope. So $\Phi(B_t)<\Phi(B)$ for small $t>0$, a contradiction.

steps.slogan: Turn the stationarity condition into the product form $B=D_1AD_2$.
steps.detail: Now $B$ is positive, so for every $E$ with zero row sums and zero column sums, $\frac d{dt}\Phi(B+tE)$ at $t=0$ is $\sum e_{kl}(\log(b_{kl}/a_{kl})+1)=0$. The matrices of the form $\lambda_k+\mu_l$ (the [Lagrange multipliers](c:lagrange-multiplier) of the margin constraints) are exactly the orthogonal complement of such $E$. So $b_{kl}=e^{\lambda_k}a_{kl}e^{\mu_l-1}$, which is $B=D_1AD_2$.

steps.slogan: Show that every doubly stochastic product form equals $B$, then compare the factors.
steps.detail: Let $B'=D_1'AD_2'$ be doubly stochastic. Then $\log(b'_{kl}/a_{kl})+1$ has the form $\lambda_k+\mu_l$, so for $C\in\mathcal D$ the slope of $\Phi$ from $B'$ toward $C$ is $0$, because $C-B'$ has zero margins. Convexity gives $\Phi(C)\ge\Phi(B')$, so $B'$ is a minimizer, and strict convexity gives $B'=B$. Then $(d'_i/d_i)(e'_j/e_j)=1$ for all $i,j$, so $d'_i=cd_i$ and $e'_j=e_j/c$.

concepts.c:diagonal-matrix: The scaling factors are the entries of two diagonal matrices.
concepts.c:doubly-stochastic-matrix: The minimization runs over this set, and the result lies in it.
concepts.c:compact-convex-set: Compactness gives a minimizer and convexity gives the segment argument.
concepts.c:strictly-convex-function: Strict convexity of the entropy makes the minimizer unique.
concepts.c:lagrange-multiplier: The numbers $\lambda_k,\mu_l$ give the diagonal factors of the scaling.

source.note: A variational proof by relative entropy minimization; Sinkhorn's original proof (Annals of Mathematical Statistics 35 (1964), 876-879) iterates row and column normalization.

statement: Take a commutative diagram in an [abelian category](c:abelian-category) with [exact](c:exact-sequence) rows $A\xrightarrow{\alpha}B\xrightarrow{\beta}C\to0$ and $0\to A'\xrightarrow{\alpha'}B'\xrightarrow{\beta'}C'$ and vertical maps $f,g,h$. Then there is a [connecting homomorphism](c:connecting-homomorphism) $\delta\colon\ker h\to\operatorname{coker}f$ that makes $\ker f\to\ker g\to\ker h\xrightarrow{\delta}\operatorname{coker}f\to\operatorname{coker}g\to\operatorname{coker}h$ exact.

hypotheses.text: The diagram lies in an [abelian category](c:abelian-category), for example in modules over a ring.
Both rows are [exact](c:exact-sequence) as shown.
The two squares commute: $g\alpha=\alpha'f$ and $h\beta=\beta'g$.

conclusion: There is a map $\delta\colon\ker h\to\operatorname{coker}f$ such that the six-term sequence of kernels and cokernels is exact.

proofs.name: Diagram chase
proofs.slogan: Chase elements through the diagram to define $\delta$ and to check exactness at the four inner places.
proofs.scope: A chase for modules; the case of an abelian category follows from the Freyd-Mitchell embedding. The four inner places are $\ker g$, $\ker h$, $\operatorname{coker}f$ and $\operatorname{coker}g$.

roles.why: It supplies kernels and cokernels, and the embedding into modules that justifies the chase.
Exactness of the rows gives the lifts and the pullbacks in every chase.
Commutativity makes the maps between kernels and cokernels well defined and makes $\delta$ well defined.

steps.slogan: Pass $f,g,h$ to kernels and cokernels by commutativity.
steps.detail: If $f(a)=0$ then $g(\alpha a)=\alpha'f(a)=0$, so $\alpha$ restricts to $\ker f\to\ker g$. In the same way $\beta$ gives $\ker g\to\ker h$. Since $\alpha'(\operatorname{im}f)\subseteq\operatorname{im}g$ and $\beta'(\operatorname{im}g)\subseteq\operatorname{im}h$, the maps $\alpha',\beta'$ descend to the [cokernels](c:kernel-and-cokernel).

steps.slogan: Define $\delta$ by lifting, applying $g$ and pulling back.
steps.detail: Take $c\in\ker h$ and choose $b$ with $\beta b=c$. Then $\beta'gb=hc=0$, so $gb=\alpha'a'$ for a unique $a'$, because $\ker\beta'=\operatorname{im}\alpha'$ and $\alpha'$ is injective. Put $\delta c=[a']$. Another lift $b+\alpha a$ changes $a'$ by $f(a)$, so $\delta$ is well defined and additive.

steps.slogan: Check exactness at $\ker g$ and at $\ker h$.
steps.detail: If $b\in\ker g$ and $\beta b=0$, then $b=\alpha a$ and $\alpha'f(a)=gb=0$, so $a\in\ker f$. If $c\in\ker h$ and $\delta c=[a']=0$, then $a'=f(a)$, and $b-\alpha a$ lies in $\ker g$ and maps to $c$. The composites are zero by construction.

steps.slogan: Check exactness at $\operatorname{coker}f$ and at $\operatorname{coker}g$.
steps.detail: If $[a']$ maps to $0$ in $\operatorname{coker}g$, then $\alpha'a'=gb$, so $c=\beta b\in\ker h$ and $\delta c=[a']$. If $[b']$ maps to $0$ in $\operatorname{coker}h$, then $\beta'b'=hc$ for some $c=\beta b$, so $b'-gb\in\ker\beta'=\operatorname{im}\alpha'$ and $[b']$ comes from $\operatorname{coker}f$. The composites are zero.

steps.slogan: Transfer the chase to any abelian category by the Freyd-Mitchell embedding.
steps.detail: The diagram lies in a small abelian subcategory. By the Freyd-Mitchell theorem, an exact and fully faithful functor embeds it in modules over a ring. Exactness and the existence of $\delta$ are detected there, so the statement holds in every abelian category.

concepts.c:abelian-category: Kernels, cokernels and the module embedding exist in an abelian category.
concepts.c:exact-sequence: Exactness of the rows drives every step of the chase.
concepts.c:connecting-homomorphism: The map $\delta$ is the connecting homomorphism that the chase builds.
concepts.c:kernel-and-cokernel: The six-term sequence consists of kernels and cokernels.

source.note: The classical diagram chase, as in Weibel, An Introduction to Homological Algebra, section 1.3 (the Snake Lemma).

statement: Let $f$ be a [strictly convex function](c:strictly-convex-function) on a convex set $S$. Let $p_1,\dots,p_m\in S$ be points that are not all equal, and let $w_1,\dots,w_m>0$ with $\sum_iw_i=1$. Then $f\big(\sum_iw_ip_i\big)<\sum_iw_if(p_i)$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is [strictly convex](c:strictly-convex-function) on the convex set $S$.
The weights satisfy $w_i>0$ and $\sum_iw_i=1$.
Each point $p_i$ lies in $S$.
Two of the points differ: $p_j\ne p_k$ for some $j,k$.

formal.difference: mathlib works over an ordered field with values in an ordered module and indexes the points by a finset; the real case is a special case. The hypotheses are the same.

proofs.name: Merge two points
proofs.slogan: Merge two distinct points into their weighted mean, apply ordinary Jensen to the merged family, and apply strict convexity to the pair.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The index set has at least two elements because two points differ; the other points may be absent.

roles.why: Strict convexity gives the strict inequality at the pair, and it implies convexity for the ordinary Jensen step.
Positive weights summing to $1$ keep the merged weights valid and make $c>0$.
Points in $S$ keep the merged mean $q$ in the [convex set](c:convex-set) $S$.
Two distinct points are the pair where convexity becomes strict.

steps.slogan: Choose two distinct points $p_j\ne p_k$ and put $c=w_j+w_k$.
steps.detail: Such a pair exists because the points are not all equal. Set $q=\frac{w_j}cp_j+\frac{w_k}cp_k$. The weights $w_j/c$ and $w_k/c$ are positive with sum $1$, so $q\in S$ because $S$ is a [convex set](c:convex-set).

steps.slogan: Replace the two points by $q$ with weight $c$.
steps.detail: Then $\sum_iw_ip_i=cq+\sum_{i\ne j,k}w_ip_i$. The new weights $c$ and $w_i$ for $i\ne j,k$ are positive with sum $1$, and all new points lie in $S$.

steps.slogan: Bound $f$ at the merged mean by Jensen's inequality for the convex function $f$.
steps.detail: A strictly convex function is a [convex function](c:convex-function), so Jensen's inequality for the merged family gives $f\big(\sum_iw_ip_i\big)\le cf(q)+\sum_{i\ne j,k}w_if(p_i)$.

steps.slogan: Bound $f(q)$ strictly by strict convexity at the pair.
steps.detail: Since $p_j\ne p_k$ and the weights $w_j/c$ and $w_k/c$ lie in $(0,1)$, strict convexity gives $f(q)<\frac{w_j}cf(p_j)+\frac{w_k}cf(p_k)$.

steps.slogan: Multiply the strict bound by $c>0$ and chain the two bounds.
steps.detail: Multiplying by $c>0$ keeps the strict sign, so $cf(q)<w_jf(p_j)+w_kf(p_k)$. Adding the remaining terms to the Jensen bound gives $f\big(\sum_iw_ip_i\big)\le cf(q)+\sum_{i\ne j,k}w_if(p_i)<\sum_iw_if(p_i)$.

concepts.c:strictly-convex-function: Strict convexity at the distinct pair makes the final inequality strict.
concepts.c:convex-set: Convexity of the set keeps the merged mean inside the domain of $f$.
concepts.c:convex-function: Ordinary convexity gives the non-strict Jensen bound for the merged family.

source.note: mathlib merges two distinct points into one with weight w j + w k, applies ConvexOn.map_add_sum_le for ordinary Jensen, and uses the strict convexity field of StrictConvexOn for the pair.

statement: Let $N$ be a linear resistive network of resistors and independent sources, with two terminals $A,B$. Suppose its equations have exactly one solution for every terminal current $i$ drawn from $A$. Let $V_{th}$ be the open-circuit voltage and $R_{th}$ the resistance seen with all sources set to zero. Then the terminal voltage is $v=V_{th}-R_{th}\,i$.

hypotheses.text: The network $N$ contains only resistors and independent voltage and current sources.
For every source setting and every terminal current $i$, the network equations have exactly one solution.

conclusion: The terminal voltage satisfies $v=V_{th}-R_{th}\,i$, so $N$ can be replaced at $A,B$ by a source $V_{th}$ in series with $R_{th}$.

proofs.name: Superposition
proofs.slogan: Write the network equations as a linear system, split the solution into a source part and a current part, and read off $V_{th}$ and $R_{th}$.
proofs.scope: Direct current resistive networks with a unique solution. The replacement is exact for every load that is connected at $A,B$ and keeps its own equations.

roles.why: Linear elements give linear network equations, which is what superposition needs.
Uniqueness lets the sum of two solutions be identified with the solution of the sum.

steps.slogan: Write the network equations as linear equations with the terminal current as an input.
steps.detail: Kirchhoff's current law, Kirchhoff's voltage law and Ohm's law are linear equations in the branch currents and voltages $x$. The source values $s$ and the terminal current $i$ appear on the right-hand side. The terminal voltage $v$ is a linear function of $x$.

steps.slogan: Show that the solution is linear in the sources and the terminal current.
steps.detail: If $x_1$ solves the equations for $(s_1,i_1)$ and $x_2$ for $(s_2,i_2)$, then $x_1+x_2$ solves them for $(s_1+s_2,i_1+i_2)$, and scaling works the same way. Uniqueness identifies $x_1+x_2$ with the solution. So $v(s,i)=v(s,0)+v(0,i)$ by [superposition](c:superposition).

steps.slogan: Identify $V_{th}$ with the terminal voltage at zero current.
steps.detail: With $i=0$ the terminals are open, so $v(s,0)$ is the open-circuit voltage $V_{th}$. It does not depend on the load.

steps.slogan: Identify the response to $i$ with all sources zero as $-R_{th}\,i$.
steps.detail: With $s=0$ each voltage source has voltage $0$ (a short circuit) and each current source has current $0$ (an open circuit). The map $i\mapsto v(0,i)$ is linear from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb R$, so $v(0,i)=-R_{th}\,i$ for a constant $R_{th}$. This constant is the resistance seen at the terminals of the network with its sources set to zero.

steps.slogan: Combine the two parts and replace $N$ in any load circuit.
steps.detail: Adding the parts gives $v=V_{th}-R_{th}\,i$. Connect any load at $A,B$. The combined solution restricted to $N$ solves the equations of $N$ for some terminal current $i$, so it obeys this relation. A source $V_{th}$ in series with $R_{th}$ obeys the same relation, so the load sees the same voltage and current.

concepts.c:superposition: Superposition splits the solution into a source part and a current part.

source.note: The standard textbook proof by superposition and uniqueness of the solution of a linear network.

statement: Every proper [filter](c:filter) $F$ on a set $X$ is contained in an [ultrafilter](c:ultrafilter) on $X$.

hypotheses.text: The set $F$ is a proper [filter](c:filter) on $X$: it is closed under finite intersections and supersets, and $\emptyset\notin F$.

conclusion: There is an ultrafilter $U$ on $X$ with $F\subseteq U$.

proofs.name: Zorn's lemma
proofs.slogan: Order the proper filters above $F$, take a maximal one by Zorn's lemma, and show that a maximal filter decides every subset.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; the hypothesis excludes $X=\emptyset$. An ultrafilter is a proper filter $U$ with $A\in U$ or $X\setminus A\in U$ for every $A\subseteq X$.

roles.why: It makes $F$ a member of the poset, and properness survives unions of chains and the extension step.

steps.slogan: Order the proper filters that contain $F$ by inclusion.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal P$ be the set of proper filters $G$ on $X$ with $F\subseteq G$, ordered by inclusion. It is nonempty because $F\in\mathcal P$.

steps.slogan: Show that every nonempty [chain](c:chain) in $\mathcal P$ has an upper bound in $\mathcal P$.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal C$ be a nonempty chain and $G=\bigcup\mathcal C$. Two members of $G$ lie in one filter of the chain, so their intersection lies in $G$. The union is closed under supersets and does not contain $\emptyset$. So $G\in\mathcal P$ bounds the chain.

steps.slogan: Take a [maximal element](c:maximal-element) $U$ of $\mathcal P$ by Zorn's lemma.
steps.detail: Every chain of $\mathcal P$ has an upper bound, so Zorn's lemma gives a maximal proper filter $U$ with $F\subseteq U$.

steps.slogan: Extend $U$ by a set $A$ whose complement is not in $U$.
steps.detail: Let $A\subseteq X$ with $X\setminus A\notin U$. Every $C\in U$ meets $A$, since $C\cap A=\emptyset$ would give $C\subseteq X\setminus A$ and hence $X\setminus A\in U$. So $U_A=\{B: B\supseteq A\cap C\text{ for some }C\in U\}$ is a proper filter that contains $U$ and $A$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $U$ contains $A$ or its complement for every $A$.
steps.detail: By maximality $U_A=U$, so $A\in U$ whenever $X\setminus A\notin U$. Hence for every $A\subseteq X$, either $A\in U$ or $X\setminus A\in U$, so $U$ is an ultrafilter containing $F$.

concepts.c:filter: The poset consists of proper filters, and unions of chains stay filters.
concepts.c:ultrafilter: A maximal proper filter is the required ultrafilter.
concepts.c:chain: Zorn's lemma needs an upper bound for every chain of filters.
concepts.c:maximal-element: The maximal proper filter is the candidate ultrafilter.

source.note: The standard application of Zorn's lemma to the poset of proper filters above $F$.

statement: Let $L$ be a [first-order](c:first-order-logic) language and $M$ an infinite $L$-structure. Let $\kappa$ be a [cardinal](c:cardinal-number) with $\kappa\ge|M|$ and $\kappa\ge$ the number of symbols of $L$. Then some $L$-structure $N$ of cardinality $\kappa$ admits an [elementary embedding](c:elementary-embedding) $M\to N$.

hypotheses.text: The $L$-structure $M$ is infinite.
The cardinal $\kappa$ satisfies $\kappa\ge|M|$.
The cardinal $\kappa$ is at least the number of symbols of $L$.

conclusion: There are an $L$-structure $N$ with $|N|=\kappa$ and an [elementary embedding](c:elementary-embedding) $M\to N$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the same theorem. It compares the cardinals through lifts across universes and counts the symbols of $L$ as L.card.

proofs.name: Elementary diagram and compactness
proofs.slogan: Build a large model of the elementary diagram of $M$ by compactness, cut it down to size $\kappa$ by downward Löwenheim-Skolem, and read off the embedding.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The language $L(M)$ adds a constant $c_m$ for each $m\in M$.

roles.why: An infinite structure has enough distinct elements to interpret any finite set of new constants.
It bounds the number of symbols of $L(M)$ by $\kappa$.
It bounds the number of symbols of $L(M)$ by $\kappa$, as the downward theorem needs.

steps.slogan: Form the elementary [diagram](c:diagram-of-a-first-order-structure) of $M$ in the language $L(M)$.
steps.detail: Let $T$ be the set of all $L(M)$-sentences true in $M$, where $c_m$ names $m$. A model $N$ of $T$ gives a map $m\mapsto c_m^N$ from $M$ to $N$, and this map is an [elementary embedding](c:elementary-embedding) of $M$ into the $L$-reduct of $N$.

steps.slogan: Find a model of the diagram with at least $\kappa$ elements by compactness.
steps.detail: Add new constants $d_\alpha$ for $\alpha<\kappa$ and the sentences $d_\alpha\ne d_\beta$ for $\alpha\ne\beta$. Every finite part has a model: $M$, with the finitely many $d_\alpha$ read as distinct elements, which exist because $M$ is infinite. By compactness the whole set has a model, and its $L(M)$-reduct $N_0$ is a model of $T$ with at least $\kappa$ elements.

steps.slogan: Cut $N_0$ down to an elementary substructure of size exactly $\kappa$.
steps.detail: The language $L(M)$ has at most $|L|+|M|\le\kappa$ symbols, and $\kappa\ge|M|\ge\aleph_0$. Since $\kappa\le|N_0|$, the downward Löwenheim-Skolem theorem gives an elementary substructure $N\preceq N_0$ with $|N|=\kappa$.

steps.slogan: Transfer the diagram to $N$ and restrict to $L$.
steps.detail: The structure $N$ is [elementarily equivalent](c:elementary-equivalence) to $N_0$ as an $L(M)$-structure, so $N$ is a model of $T$. By the first step, $m\mapsto c_m^N$ is an elementary embedding of $M$ into the $L$-reduct of $N$, which has cardinality $\kappa$.

concepts.c:first-order-logic: The theorem is about structures of a first-order language.
concepts.c:cardinal-number: The cardinal $\kappa$ is the size of the model that the proof builds.
concepts.c:elementary-embedding: The embedding of $M$ is read off from a model of its elementary diagram.
concepts.c:diagram-of-a-first-order-structure: Models of the elementary diagram are the structures that receive an elementary embedding of $M$.
concepts.c:elementary-equivalence: An elementary substructure satisfies the same sentences as the big model.

source.note: mathlib takes a large model of L.elementaryDiagram M (exists_large_model_of_infinite_model), cuts it with exists_elementaryEmbedding_card_eq_of_le, and applies ElementaryEmbedding.ofModelsElementaryDiagram.

statement: A finite graph is [planar](c:planar-graph) if and only if it has neither the [complete graph](c:complete-graph) $K_5$ nor the complete [bipartite graph](c:bipartite-graph) $K_{3,3}$ as a [minor](c:graph-minor).

hypotheses.text: The graph $G$ is finite and simple.

conclusion: The graph $G$ is planar exactly when $K_5$ and $K_{3,3}$ are not minors of $G$.

proofs.name: From Kuratowski's theorem
proofs.slogan: Show that planarity is minor-closed and that $K_5$ and $K_{3,3}$ are not planar, then pass from minors to subdivisions and apply Kuratowski's theorem.
proofs.scope: Finite simple graphs. The converse direction rests on Kuratowski's theorem, which this proof cites and does not repeat.

roles.why: Finiteness gives the vertex and edge counts of Euler's formula and the contraction steps.

steps.slogan: Show that deleting and contracting preserve [planarity](c:planar-graph).
steps.detail: Deleting a vertex or an edge from a plane drawing leaves a plane drawing. Contracting an edge $uv$ shrinks the edge to a point along the drawing, which keeps the drawing plane. A [minor](c:graph-minor) arises by such operations, so every minor of a planar graph is planar.

steps.slogan: Show that $K_5$ and $K_{3,3}$ are not planar by an edge count.
steps.detail: By Euler's formula, a plane simple graph with $v\ge3$ vertices has at most $3v-6$ edges, and at most $2v-4$ edges if it is [bipartite](c:bipartite-graph), since every face has at least four boundary edges. $K_5$ has $10>9$ edges and $K_{3,3}$ has $9>8$ edges.

steps.slogan: Conclude that a planar graph has neither $K_5$ nor $K_{3,3}$ as a minor.
steps.detail: If a planar graph had such a minor, that minor would be planar by the first step. This contradicts the second step.

steps.slogan: Show that a subdivision of $H$ contains $H$ as a minor.
steps.detail: Contract all but one edge of each subdivided path of a subdivision of $H$. This gives $H$. So a graph with a subgraph that is a subdivision of $K_5$ or $K_{3,3}$ has $K_5$ or $K_{3,3}$ as a minor.

steps.slogan: Apply Kuratowski's theorem to a graph with no $K_5$ and no $K_{3,3}$ minor.
steps.detail: Let $G$ have neither minor. By the previous step $G$ has no subgraph that is a subdivision of $K_5$ or $K_{3,3}$. Kuratowski's theorem says that a finite graph without such a subgraph is planar, so $G$ is planar.

steps.slogan: Join the two directions into the equivalence.
steps.detail: The forward step shows that planar graphs have neither minor. The converse step shows that graphs with neither minor are planar. Together they give the equivalence.

concepts.c:planar-graph: Planarity is the property that is preserved by minors and characterized by them.
concepts.c:complete-graph: The graph $K_5$ is the first forbidden minor.
concepts.c:bipartite-graph: The graph $K_{3,3}$ is bipartite, which sharpens the edge count.
concepts.c:graph-minor: The theorem characterizes planarity by the minor relation.

source.note: The standard derivation of the minor form from Kuratowski's subdivision form; see Diestel, Graph Theory, section 4.4.

statement: Every [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ of dimension $m>0$ that is Hausdorff and second countable admits a smooth [embedding](c:embedding-of-differentiable-manifolds) into $\mathbb R^{2m}$.

hypotheses.text: The space $M$ is a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) of dimension $m$.
The space $M$ is Hausdorff and [second countable](c:second-countable-space).
The dimension satisfies $m>0$.

conclusion: There is a smooth embedding $M\to\mathbb R^{2m}$.

formal.difference: The declaration treats only compact manifolds and gives a smooth closed embedding with injective derivative into some Euclidean space $\mathbb R^n$, not into $\mathbb R^{2m}$.

proofs.name: Weak embedding and the Whitney trick
proofs.slogan: Embed in a large Euclidean space by bump functions, project down to $\mathbb R^{2m+1}$ by a generic direction, then remove double points in $\mathbb R^{2m}$ by Whitney's trick.
proofs.scope: An outline of Whitney's published proof, for $m\ge2$, with $m=1$ done by hand. The steps that rest on the cited papers are the generic projection and the Whitney trick.

roles.why: Charts and bump functions of the smooth structure build the first embedding.
Second countability gives a finite cover by unions of coordinate balls and a proper function.
For $m\ge2$ the Whitney trick applies; for $m=1$ the classification of curves gives the embedding.

steps.slogan: Embed $M$ in some $\mathbb R^N$ by gluing finitely many bump-function charts.
steps.detail: Second countability gives a finite cover by open sets that are disjoint unions of coordinate balls. With bump functions $\rho_i$ and charts $\phi_i$, the map $x\mapsto(\rho_i\phi_i,\rho_i)_i$ is an injective immersion, and a proper smooth function as an extra coordinate makes it an embedding. For compact $M$ this is the route of mathlib's exists_embedding_euclidean_of_compact.

steps.slogan: Project along generic directions until $N=2m+1$.
steps.detail: For $N>2m+1$, the tangent and secant directions of the image form a set of dimension at most $2m$ in the $(N-1)$-dimensional projective space. By Sard's theorem this set has measure zero, so a generic projection of an [immersion](c:immersion) stays an injective immersion. Properness survives because the proper coordinate is kept.

steps.slogan: Project once more to an immersion into $\mathbb R^{2m}$ with only transverse double points.
steps.detail: An embedding into $\mathbb R^{2m+1}$ projects to an immersion into $\mathbb R^{2m}$ along any direction outside the tangent directions, which form a set of dimension $2m-1$. A small perturbation gives [transversality](c:transversality), so the double points are isolated and transverse.

steps.slogan: Remove the double points in pairs by the Whitney trick when $m\ge2$.
steps.detail: Join two double points of opposite sign by a path in $M$, and push one sheet off the other along a Whitney disk that the path bounds. A local kink creates a double point of the opposite sign when two points have the same sign. Whitney (1944) carries this out for every $m\ge2$.

steps.slogan: Embed the case $m=1$ in the plane by hand.
steps.detail: By the classification of one-dimensional manifolds, every component is a circle or a line. Place the circles with small radius at the points $(2k,0)$ and the lines along $x=2k+1$, with a different integer $k$ for each component. The images are disjoint and locally finite.

steps.slogan: Join the case $m=1$ and the case $m\ge2$.
steps.detail: For $m\ge2$ the first four steps give a smooth embedding into $\mathbb R^{2m}$. For $m=1$ the last step gives one. So every such manifold of dimension $m>0$ embeds in $\mathbb R^{2m}$.

concepts.c:smooth-manifold: The charts of the smooth structure build the first embedding.
concepts.c:embedding-of-differentiable-manifolds: The goal is a smooth map that is a homeomorphism onto a submanifold.
concepts.c:second-countable-space: It gives a finite cover by coordinate balls and a proper function.
concepts.c:immersion: Projections must keep the map an injective immersion.
concepts.c:transversality: Transverse double points are isolated, which lets the Whitney trick remove them.

source.ref: H. Whitney, The self-intersections of a smooth n-manifold in 2n-space, Annals of Mathematics 45 (1944), 220-246
source.note: Steps 1 and 2 are the weak theorem of Whitney's 1936 paper Differentiable manifolds (Annals of Mathematics 37); for compact manifolds step 1 is the route of mathlib's exists_embedding_euclidean_of_compact.

statement: Let $F\subseteq E$ be fields. Suppose $x\in E$ lies in the smallest subfield of $E$ that contains $F$ and contains $y$ whenever it contains $y^n$ for some $n\ge1$. Then the [Galois group](c:galois-group) of the [minimal polynomial](c:minimal-polynomial) of $x$ over $F$ is a [solvable group](c:solvable-group).

hypotheses.text: The fields satisfy $F\subseteq E$, a [field extension](c:field-extension).
The element $x$ lies in the smallest subfield of $E$ that contains $F$ and is closed under taking $n$-th roots in $E$ for $n\ge1$.

conclusion: The Galois group of the minimal polynomial of $x$ over $F$, the automorphism group of its splitting field over $F$, is solvable.

proofs.name: Induction over radical closure
proofs.slogan: Show that the elements with a solvable Galois group form a subfield closed under radicals, using splitting fields for sums, products and roots.
proofs.scope: Any characteristic. The Galois group of a polynomial is the group of automorphisms of its splitting field over $F$.

roles.why: The subfield between $F$ and $E$ and the minimal polynomials live in this extension.
The element $x$ lies in the radical closure, which sits inside the set that the proof builds.

steps.slogan: Set up induction on the smallest subfield closed under radicals.
steps.detail: Let $S$ be the set of elements of that subfield whose minimal polynomial has a solvable group. Every element of the subfield is algebraic over $F$, so minimal polynomials exist. If $S$ contains $F$, is closed under sums and products, and contains $y$ whenever it contains $y^n$, then $S$ is a subfield of algebraic elements closed under radicals.

steps.slogan: Show that elements of $F$ have a trivial Galois group.
steps.detail: For $a\in F$ the minimal polynomial is $X-a$, whose [splitting field](c:is-splitting-field) is $F$. Its automorphism group over $F$ is trivial, hence solvable.

steps.slogan: Pass to sums and products through the splitting field of the product of two minimal polynomials.
steps.detail: Let $p,q$ be the minimal polynomials of $x,y\in S$, and $L$ the splitting field of $pq$. For $z=x+y$ or $z=xy$, the field $F(x,y)$ embeds in $L$ over $F$, and the image of $z$ has the same minimal polynomial. So $\mathrm{Gal}(\mu_z)$ is a quotient of $\mathrm{Aut}(L/F)$, which embeds in $\mathrm{Gal}(p)\times\mathrm{Gal}(q)$.

steps.slogan: Show that $X^n-a$ has a solvable Galois group over every field.
steps.detail: Let $L'$ be the splitting field of $X^n-a$ with $a\ne0$, and $L\subseteq L'$ the field generated by the $n$-th roots of unity. Automorphisms act on the cyclic group of these roots, so $\mathrm{Aut}(L/F)$ is abelian. An element of $\mathrm{Aut}(L'/L)$ sends a root $\beta$ to $\zeta\beta$ with $\zeta^n=1$, so $\mathrm{Aut}(L'/L)$ is cyclic. An extension of solvable groups is solvable.

steps.slogan: Pass to $n$-th roots through the tower from the splitting field of $p$ to that of $p(X^n)$.
steps.detail: Let $x^n\in S$ with minimal polynomial $p$, and $K$ the splitting field of $p$. The minimal polynomial of $x$ divides $p(X^n)$, and over $K$ this polynomial is a constant times $\prod_i(X^n-r_i)$, whose group is solvable by the previous step. So $\mathrm{Gal}(p(X^n))$ is an extension of $\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$ by a solvable group, and its quotient $\mathrm{Gal}(\mu_x)$ is solvable.

steps.slogan: Conclude from the minimality of the radical closure.
steps.detail: By the steps above $S$ contains $F$, is closed under sums, products and radicals, and is a subfield. So $S$ contains the smallest such subfield, which contains $x$. Hence the Galois group of the minimal polynomial of $x$ is solvable.

concepts.c:galois-group: Solvability of this group is the property that the induction carries along.
concepts.c:minimal-polynomial: The group is attached to the minimal polynomial of $x$ over $F$.
concepts.c:solvable-group: Sums, products and radicals each preserve solvability of the groups.
concepts.c:field-extension: The element $x$ and the intermediate fields live in the extension $E/F$.
concepts.c:is-splitting-field: The Galois group is the automorphism group of a splitting field.

source.note: mathlib inducts with solvableByRad.induction, using induction_step for sums and products, induction_rad for radicals, gal_X_pow_sub_C_isSolvable for $X^n-a$ and gal_isSolvable_tower for towers.

statement: Let $f\colon X\to Y$ be a [measurable function](c:measurable-function) from a [measurable space](c:measurable-space) $X$ to a [separable](c:separable-space) metric space $Y$ with its Borel $\sigma$-algebra. Then there are [simple functions](c:simple-function) $f_n\colon X\to Y$ with $f_n(x)\to f(x)$ for every $x$, that is, $f_n\to f$ [pointwise](c:pointwise-convergence).

hypotheses.text: The map $f$ is [measurable](c:measurable-function) for the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $Y$.
The metric space $Y$ is [separable](c:separable-space).

conclusion: Simple functions $f_n$ exist with $f_n(x)\to f(x)$ for every $x\in X$.

formal.difference: The declaration fixes a separable subset $s$ of the target with a base point $y_0\in s$, and states convergence of the explicit sequence approxOn at each $x$ with $f(x)\in\overline s$. This statement takes $s=Y$ and asserts only that such a sequence exists.

proofs.name: Nearest dense point
proofs.slogan: Choose a dense sequence in the target, send each value to its nearest point among the first $n+1$ dense points, and compose with $f$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. If $X=\emptyset$ there is nothing to prove, so let $X$ and hence $Y$ be nonempty; a simple function is measurable with finite range.

roles.why: Measurability of $f$ makes each composite $N_n\circ f$ measurable.
Separability supplies the countable dense set that the nearest-point maps use.

steps.slogan: Choose a [dense](c:dense-set) sequence $d_0,d_1,\dots$ in $Y$.
steps.detail: Because $Y$ is separable and nonempty, it has a countable dense subset. Enumerate it as a sequence $d_0,d_1,\dots$, repeating points if the subset is finite.

steps.slogan: Send each point of $Y$ to its nearest point among $d_0,\dots,d_n$.
steps.detail: Define $N_n(y)=d_k$, where $k\le n$ is the least index that minimizes $\mathrm{dist}(y,d_k)$. The map $N_n$ takes at most $n+1$ values.

steps.slogan: Show that each nearest-point map $N_n$ is a [Borel](c:borel-set) function.
steps.detail: The set $\{y:N_n(y)=d_k\}$ is defined by finitely many inequalities between the continuous functions $\mathrm{dist}(\cdot,d_j)$. So it is a Borel set, and $N_n$ is measurable with finite range.

steps.slogan: Compose with $f$ to get the [simple functions](c:simple-function) $f_n=N_n\circ f$.
steps.detail: A composite of measurable maps is measurable, and $f_n$ takes at most $n+1$ values. So each $f_n$ is a simple function from $X$ to $Y$.

steps.slogan: Show that $f_n(x)\to f(x)$ by density.
steps.detail: Fix $x$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Density gives $k$ with $\mathrm{dist}(f(x),d_k)<\varepsilon$. For $n\ge k$ the nearest point satisfies $\mathrm{dist}(f_n(x),f(x))\le\mathrm{dist}(d_k,f(x))<\varepsilon$.

concepts.c:measurable-function: The map $f$ must be measurable so that the composites are.
concepts.c:measurable-space: The simple functions are measurable on this domain.
concepts.c:separable-space: A countable dense set exists exactly because the target is separable.
concepts.c:simple-function: The approximants are measurable with finite range.
concepts.c:pointwise-convergence: The sequence converges at every point of the domain.
concepts.c:dense-set: Density gives a dense point close to each value of $f$.
concepts.c:borel-set: The pieces of the nearest-point map are Borel sets.

source.note: mathlib composes f with SimpleFunc.nearestPt of a dense sequence (approxOn) and proves convergence with tendsto_nearestPt.

statement: The value $\zeta(3)=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-3}$ of the [Riemann zeta function](c:riemann-zeta-function) is an [irrational number](c:irrational-number).
conclusion: The number $\zeta(3)$ is not a quotient of two integers.

proofs.name: Beukers integrals
proofs.slogan: Build integrals of Legendre polynomials that are small linear forms in $1$ and $\zeta(3)$ with controlled denominators, and contradict rationality.
proofs.scope: An outline of Beukers' proof of Apéry's theorem. The integral computations and bounds rest on the cited paper.

steps.slogan: Define the integrals $I_n$ with shifted [Legendre polynomials](c:legendre-polynomial).
steps.detail: Let $P_n(x)=\frac1{n!}\frac{d^n}{dx^n}\big(x^n(1-x)^n\big)$, a polynomial with integer coefficients. Put $I_n=\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1\frac{-\log(xy)}{1-xy}P_n(x)P_n(y)\,dx\,dy$. For $n=0$ the integral is $I_0=2\zeta(3)$.

steps.slogan: Show that $I_n=(a_n+b_n\zeta(3))/d_n^3$ with integers $a_n,b_n$.
steps.detail: Expand $\frac1{1-xy}$ as a geometric series. Then $\iint\frac{-\log(xy)}{1-xy}x^ry^s\,dx\,dy$ equals $2\big(\zeta(3)-\sum_{m\le r}m^{-3}\big)$ for $r=s$ and a rational number with denominator dividing $d_n^3$ for $r\ne s$, where $d_n=\mathrm{lcm}(1,\dots,n)$. Summing over the integer coefficients of $P_n(x)P_n(y)$ gives the form.

steps.slogan: Rewrite $I_n$ as a triple integral by integrating by parts.
steps.detail: Write $\frac{-\log(xy)}{1-xy}=\int_0^1\frac{dz}{1-(1-xy)z}$. Rodrigues' formula, $n$ integrations by parts in $x$ and in $y$, and the substitution $w=\frac{1-z}{1-(1-xy)z}$ give $I_n=\iiint_{[0,1]^3}\Big(\frac{x(1-x)y(1-y)w(1-w)}{1-(1-xy)w}\Big)^n\frac{dx\,dy\,dw}{1-(1-xy)w}$.

steps.slogan: Bound the integrand to get $0<I_n<2\zeta(3)(\sqrt2-1)^{4n}$.
steps.detail: On $[0,1]^3$ the factor $\frac{x(1-x)y(1-y)w(1-w)}{1-(1-xy)w}$ has maximum $(\sqrt2-1)^4$. The remaining integral $\iiint\frac{dx\,dy\,dw}{1-(1-xy)w}$ equals $2\zeta(3)$. So $I_n$ is positive and less than $2\zeta(3)(\sqrt2-1)^{4n}$.

steps.slogan: Compare $d_n^3I_n$ with the integers $qa_n+pb_n$ to contradict rationality.
steps.detail: By the prime number theorem $d_n=e^{n(1+o(1))}$, and $e^3(\sqrt2-1)^4<0.6$, so $d_n^3I_n\to0$. If $\zeta(3)=p/q$, then $q\,d_n^3I_n=qa_n+pb_n$ is a positive integer for every $n$. A positive integer cannot tend to $0$, so $\zeta(3)$ is irrational.

concepts.c:riemann-zeta-function: The integrals are small linear forms in $1$ and its value $\zeta(3)$.
concepts.c:irrational-number: The proof shows that the value is not a quotient of integers.
concepts.c:legendre-polynomial: Their integer coefficients and Rodrigues formula control the arithmetic and the bound.

source.ref: F. Beukers, A note on the irrationality of zeta(2) and zeta(3), Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society 11 (1979), 268-272
source.note: Beukers recasts Apery's 1978 proof with integrals of Legendre polynomials.
